deep.reconstruction:
This page has no mathematics. It is a clean-copy page of lecture notes on ancient (Hebrew) history, continuing from the previous page (Saul, David, Ishbosheth) into the next (Solomon, the division of the kingdom, 975-588 BC). The style and content match a university course on ancient history in the Heeren/Göttingen tradition. The hand and content suggest a student's notebook kept with the Gauss papers rather than Gauss's own research notes, though authorship cannot be settled from this page.

Content, in order:
(1) David becomes king of the whole nation at age 30.
(2) He makes Jerusalem the new capital and central point of the nation, a place the notes say had not been prominent before.
(3) He moves the Tabernacle (Stiftshütte) to Jerusalem and plans a temple to Jehovah.
(4) The 'King of Mesopotamia' had subjected much of Syria. David defeats him and subjugates Syria (biblically Hadadezer of Zobah and his Aramean allies, 2 Sam 8 and 10).
(5) David defeats the Edomites and extends his conquests to the Arabian Gulf (Gulf of Aqaba / Red Sea).
(6) A census figure in parentheses: Judah 500,000 and Israel 800,000 men fit for war. This matches 2 Sam 24:9.
(7) In his last years his sons rebel (Absalom).
(8) David dies in his 70th year, dated 1015 (BC, traditional chronology).
(9) Solomon succeeds him, with his brother Adonijah as a rival claimant.
(10) Under Solomon government becomes much more absolute, and the realm is reorganised into 12 parts, each with a governor. The next page adds that each supplied the king for one month a year (cf. 1 Kings 4:7).

There are no derivations to reconstruct. The only quantitative content is chronological and demographic arithmetic, which I supply as implicit consistency checks:
- 30 + 40 years of reign = 70.
- 1055 (Saul's death, previous page) - 1015 (David's death) = 40.
- 1015 - 975 (Solomon's death, next page) = 40 years for Solomon.
- 500,000 + 800,000 = 1,300,000 fighting men.
errors: Historical simplification, not a mathematical error: the adversary called 'König von Mesopotamien' is biblically Hadadezer king of Zobah (an Aramean state), supported by Arameans from beyond the Euphrates. 'Mesopotamia' is loose.
The 12 administrative districts under Solomon (1 Kings 4:7-19) do not coincide exactly with the 12 tribes. Calling them '12 Stämme' is a simplification.

Chronology: dates of 1055/1015/975 BC follow the older traditional (Ussher-type) reckoning. Modern estimates put David's death c. 970 and Solomon's c. 931 BC. This is consistent for its period and not an error of the writer.

results.what: Lecture-note narrative of the reigns of David and Solomon, with traditional dates and the census figures of 2 Sam 24:9
results.modern_name: Ancient Near Eastern / biblical history (Göttingen universal-history lecture tradition)
results.usually_credited_to: Standard 18th/19th-century historical lecture material (e.g., A. H. L. Heeren, Göttingen), based on the Hebrew Bible

deep.surprise_reason: The page contains no mathematics at all: it is routine historical lecture notes, probably not even authored by Gauss. Its presence in a Gauss bundle is archivally mildly interesting but mathematically insignificant.

checkable.asserts: Total fighting men in Judah plus Israel per the census figures on the page
David king at 30, reigning 40 years, dies in his 70th year, consistent with the page
Interval from Saul's death (c. 1055, previous page) to David's death (1015) equals David's 40-year reign
Solomon's reign from 1015 to 975 (next page) is 40 years, matching 1 Kings 11:42

transcription_corrections: Line 5: 'das bis dahin nie bekannt geworden war' — the image looks more like 'bekannt gewesen war' (reading uncertain).
Line 6: 'und beschloss[?]' — the image reads more plausibly 'und suchte' (… dem Jehovah einen Tempel zu erbauen).
Line 13: 'Einwohner in Juda' — the manuscript abbreviates as 'Jud. ä' / 'Judä' (Judäa); meaning unchanged.
Line 16: the name is written 'Absalon' in the manuscript (not 'Absalom'), as transcribed — correct.
